templates.pattern: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. A star is [T] light years away from Earth. Calculate the distance to the star in metres. (1 light year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m)
templates.explanation:
Distance = number of light years × distance per light year
= [T] × 9.46 × 10¹⁵
= [RESULT] m

A light year is the distance light travels in one year. Proxima Centauri, our nearest star, is about 4.2 light years away.

templates.pattern: A planet orbits a star at a radius of [R] × 10¹⁰ m with an orbital period of [T] × 10⁶ s. Calculate the orbital speed of the planet in m/s.
templates.explanation:
Orbital speed v = 2πr ÷ T
= 2π × [R] × 10¹⁰ ÷ ([T] × 10⁶)
= 2 × 3.14159 × [R] × 10⁴ ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] m/s

Orbital speed is the speed needed to maintain a circular orbit. Planets closer to their star orbit faster because the gravitational force is stronger.

templates.pattern: Two objects of mass [M1] × 10²⁴ kg and [M2] × 10²⁴ kg are separated by a distance of [R] × 10¹⁰ m. Calculate the gravitational force between them in newtons. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
Gravitational force F = GMm ÷ r²
= 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M1] × 10²⁴ × [M2] × 10²⁴ ÷ ([R] × 10¹⁰)²
= [RESULT] N

Gravity is a long range force that acts between all objects with mass. It decreases with the square of distance — doubling the distance reduces the force to one quarter.

templates.pattern: A planet has a mass of [M] × 10²⁴ kg and a radius of [R] × 10⁶ m. Calculate the surface gravitational field strength of the planet in N/kg. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
Surface gravity g = GM ÷ r²
= 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10²⁴ ÷ ([R] × 10⁶)²
= [RESULT] N/kg

Earth's surface gravity is 9.81 N/kg. A more massive planet or one with a smaller radius will have stronger surface gravity.

templates.pattern: A rocket needs to escape from a planet of mass [M] × 10²⁴ kg and radius [R] × 10⁶ m. Calculate the escape velocity in m/s. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
Escape velocity v = √(2GM ÷ r)
= √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10²⁴ ÷ ([R] × 10⁶))
= [RESULT] m/s

Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape a planet's gravitational field without further propulsion. Earth's escape velocity is about 11,200 m/s.

templates.pattern: A star has a diameter of [D] × 10⁹ m and is [DIST] × 10¹⁸ m away. Calculate the angular diameter of the star in radians.
templates.explanation:
Angular diameter θ = actual diameter ÷ distance
= [D] × 10⁹ ÷ ([DIST] × 10¹⁸)
= [D] ÷ ([DIST] × 10⁹)
= [RESULT] radians

Angular diameter is the apparent size of an object as seen from Earth. Even the nearest stars have very small angular diameters due to their enormous distances.

templates.pattern: A star has a parallax angle of [P] × 10⁻³ arcseconds. Calculate the distance to the star in parsecs.
templates.explanation:
Distance in parsecs d = 1 ÷ p (arcseconds)
= 1 ÷ ([P] × 10⁻³)
= 1000 ÷ [P]
= [RESULT] parsecs

The parsec is defined so that a star at 1 parsec has a parallax of 1 arcsecond. Parallax is the only direct method of measuring stellar distances.

templates.pattern: A star has a radius of [R] × 10⁸ m and a surface temperature of [T] × 10³ K. Calculate the luminosity of the star in units of 10²⁵ watts. (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴)
templates.explanation:
Luminosity L = 4πr²σT⁴
= 4π × ([R] × 10⁸)² × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × ([T] × 10³)⁴
= 4 × 3.14159 × [R]² × 10¹⁶ × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × [T]⁴ × 10¹²
= [RESULT] × 10²⁵ W

Luminosity depends strongly on temperature — doubling the temperature increases luminosity 16 times. This is because L ∝ T⁴.

templates.pattern: A galaxy is [D] × 10²² m away from Earth. Calculate the time taken for light to travel from the galaxy to Earth in years. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s)
templates.explanation:
Travel time = distance ÷ speed of light
= [D] × 10²² ÷ (3 × 10⁸)
= [D] × 10²² ÷ (3 × 10⁸ × 3.15 × 10⁷) years
= [RESULT] years

When we observe distant galaxies we are seeing them as they were millions or billions of years ago. We are looking back in time.

templates.pattern: A planet orbits a star at a radius of [R] × 10¹⁰ m at a speed of [V] × 10³ m/s. Calculate the orbital period of the planet in seconds.
templates.explanation:
Orbital period T = 2πr ÷ v
= 2π × [R] × 10¹⁰ ÷ ([V] × 10³)
= 2 × 3.14159 × [R] × 10⁷ ÷ [V]
= [RESULT] s

The orbital period is the time for one complete revolution around the star. Planets further from their star have longer orbital periods — Kepler's third law.
